146 %.finding: In December 2011, during coverage of the parliamentary elections, the state channel Rossiya-24 displayed a graphic showing 146% of voters in Rostov Oblast supporting United Russia — a mathematical impossibility. The figure was instantly nicknamed 'Churov's number' (after election-commission head Vladimir Churov) and became a meme for absurdly inflated official claims and rigged statistics. In a 2013 biography of Durov/VKontakte, '146%' signals the reader that some official or PR number should be read with mockery, not trust. By 2013 it was fully established internet slang, recognizable to any Runet user.

rendering.en: 146 percent (a Russian meme for impossibly inflated official statistics)
rendering.zh: 146%（俄罗斯网络流行语，讽刺官方夸大到荒谬的统计数字）
rendering.ja: 146パーセント（ロシアのネット・ミーム。ありえないほど水増しされた公式統計を皮肉る表現）

146 %.rationale: The bare number is meaningless outside the Runet, so denotation is kept literally but a brief in-line gloss carries the mocking connotation; register shifts from pure meme shorthand to ironic-but-explicit, sacrificing the insider wink in all three languages.

23 февраля.finding: In Russian public life 23 February is Defender of the Fatherland Day (День защитника Отечества), a federal holiday marking the 1918 founding of the Red Army and honouring the armed forces. By the 2000s–2010s it had also become the unofficial ‘men’s day’ counterpart to 8 March, with gifts, toasts and office parties; a Russian reader in 2013 would hear the date as that holiday, not a random winter day.

rendering.ja: 2月23日（祖国防衛の日）

23 февраля.rationale: Keep the calendar date and add the holiday name so denotation and the men’s-day/military connotation travel; a long Soviet-history footnote is sacrificed for biography register.

239-я школа.finding: Now the Presidential Physics-Mathematics Lyceum No. 239 in St Petersburg, one of the USSR's first specialized math schools (since 1961), long famed for producing olympiad champions and elite math/physics graduates. For a Russian reader in 2013 the number '239' alone signals top-tier academic prestige, similar to naming a famous magnet school; it is Durov's alma mater and marks him as part of an elite scientific pedigree.

rendering.en: School No. 239 (a top physics-mathematics school in St Petersburg)
rendering.zh: 第239中学(圣彼得堡著名数理重点中学)
rendering.ja: 第239校(サンクトペテルブルクの名門理数系学校)

239-я школа.rationale: Preserves denotation (the numbered school) consistently across the book while adding a brief descriptive gloss on first mention to carry the connotation of elite/olympiad prestige that the bare number conveys to Russian readers but not to foreign ones; register kept neutral/factual as in a business biography.

31-е числа.finding: In 2009–2013 Russian usage, «31-е числа» is not a calendar oddity but shorthand for Strategy-31 (Стратегия-31): civic rallies held at 18:00 on every 31st of a 31-day month (starting 31 May/July 2009, typically on Moscow’s Triumfalnaya Square) to claim Article 31 of the RF Constitution—the right of peaceful assembly. Eduard Limonov initiated them; Helsinki Group, Memorial and others joined. Authorities routinely banned and dispersed the actions; the name itself is “chapter-verse branding.” A 2013 VK/Durov reader would hear opposition street politics and police kettling, not a date.
31-е числа.rationale: Denotation of the Article-31 protest series is kept by naming Strategy-31 in parentheses; the compressed Russian allusion is sacrificed so English, Chinese and Japanese biography readers do not read a nonsense date.

9 Мая.finding: «9 Мая» означает День Победы — российский государственный праздник победы СССР над нацистской Германией в Великой Отечественной войне, отмечаемый 9 мая из-за московского времени вступления капитуляции в силу. Для российского читателя около 2013 года одна дата уже однозначно называла эмоционально значимый праздник военной памяти и национальной гордости, связанный с советскими жертвами, парадами и государственной символикой. Поэтому антисталинские публикации в этот день воспринимались не просто как исторический комментарий, а как намеренная провокация против праздничного патриотического консенсуса.

rendering.ja: 5月9日の対独戦勝記念日

9 Мая.rationale: The renderings preserve the date, identify the Russian/Soviet victory being commemorated, and avoid confusion with other countries’ victory days. They sacrifice the Russian original’s effortless metonymy and some of its immediate patriotic-emotional charge in favor of clarity for foreign readers.

Astrum.finding: Astrum is Astrum Online Entertainment (Аструм Онлайн Энтертейнмент), a Russian IT/gaming holding founded in December 2007 that consolidated online-game studios and publishers (Nival Online, IT Territory, Time Zero, Nikita Online, DJ Games). Around 2009 it was absorbed into the gaming division of Mail.ru Group, so a 2013 Russian reader reading 'Astrum' knew it as the gaming arm that had been folded into the Mail.ru gaming business. It connoted online/multiplayer games rather than any consumer-facing brand.

rendering.ja: アストラム

Astrum.rationale: It is a proper noun of a minor holding company with no established Chinese or Japanese rendering; I keep the Latin form as the denotative anchor in en/zh (glossing as the entertainment holding) and katakana in ja to preserve pronunciation and business register, sacrificing Chinese-language intuibility.

Astrum / Мацанюк / Чумаченко / Game Insi.finding: Astrum Online Entertainment was a Moscow game-holding founded by Igor Matsanyuk; Alisa Chumacheko (also given as Matsanyuk, his wife/associate) was VP of marketing there before co-founding Game Insight in 2010, a mobile/social game publisher (later HQ in Vilnius). For a 2013 Russian reader these were recognizable names in the RuNet gaming-business scene, tied to VKontakte's game-platform ecosystem and mail.ru-adjacent entrepreneurs; the register is business-journalistic, not slangy.

rendering.zh: Astrum／马察纽克／丘马琴科／Game Insight
rendering.ja: Astrum／マツァニューク／チュマチェンコ／Game Insight

Astrum / Мацанюк / Чумаченко / Game Insi.rationale: Preserved denotation (real company/person names, English brand name kept as-is) and neutral business register across languages, sacrificing any connotative RuNet-insider flavor since these are proper nouns best rendered via standard transliteration consistent with prior segments.

Delta Private Equity Partners.finding: Delta Private Equity Partners was the private-equity/venture-capital arm (originally Delta Capital Management, renamed in 2004) of The U.S. Russia Investment Fund (TUSRIF), a U.S. government-backed fund founded in 1995 with USAID money to invest in the post-Soviet Russian economy. Chaired and run by Patricia Cloherty, it made direct equity investments in Russian financial services, consumer, media and telecom companies (including Runet internet businesses) and was among the early Western institutional investors active during the period VKontakte was growing. It was purchased by UFG Private Equity, a Deutsche Bank subsidiary, around 2009, so by 2013 the name read to Russian readers as 'a US-backed Western investment fund that backed early Russian tech and internet ventures.'

rendering.ja: デルタ・プライベート・エクイティ・パートナーズ

Delta Private Equity Partners.rationale: It is a proper-noun official English firm name with no established non-Latin rendering in the target markets, so it is preserved verbatim in en and zh (Latin script is normal in Chinese business prose for foreign fund names); in ja the standard serious-business-biography practice is katakana transliteration, which keeps denotation and pronunciation but sacrifices the visual link to the original brand.

DST.finding: DST (Digital Sky Technologies) was Yuri Milner's investment firm, founded 2005/2006, which became a major early investor in Russian internet companies including VKontakte and later renamed itself Mail.ru Group in 2010 (and eventually VK). For Russian readers in 2013 it denoted the dominant, somewhat controversial consolidating investor in the Runet, associated with Milner's aggressive buyouts and later international fund DST Global. It carried connotation of consolidation/corporate power rather than being a mere technical acronym.

rendering.zh: DST（数字天空科技，尤里·米尔纳旗下投资公司）
rendering.ja: DST（デジタル・スカイ・テクノロジーズ、ユーリ・ミルナーの投資会社）

DST.rationale: Preserved denotation (full company name and identity as Milner's investment vehicle) across all three, sacrificing brevity to add a brief identifying gloss for zh/ja readers unfamiliar with Runet business history; register kept formal/neutral as befits a business biography.

DST Deal.finding: The phrase almost certainly refers to the 2007 transaction in which Yuri Milner's Digital Sky Technologies bought a 24.99% stake in VKontakte from its founders, including Pavel Durov. For a Russian reader around 2013, 'DST Deal' also carried Milner's signature style: a large late-stage stake bought quickly at a generous valuation, with no board seat or operational demands, repeated soon after with Facebook in 2009. It connoted founder-friendly capital and a stamp of legitimacy for the network.

rendering.ja: DST方式の取引

DST Deal.rationale: All three preserve the shorthand and Milner's investor brand; English expands the acronym for a reader with no Russian context (sacrificing brevity), while Chinese and Japanese add 'style/method' to convey the characteristic deal form rather than a literal 'deal', matching the insider connotation without a footnote.

Durov.com Club, Ilya Perekopsky, Vice Pr.term: Durov.com Club, Ilya Perekopsky, Vice President / Pavel Durov, President
Durov.com Club, Ilya Perekopsky, Vice Pr.finding: This is the English-language wording printed on business cards for Durov’s student-era Durov.com Club, not the formal name of a documented university institution. Durov.com was one of Pavel Durov’s nonprofit projects at Saint Petersburg State University; the club’s English name and corporate titles styled an informal campus circle after selective, elite Western student clubs such as Harvard’s final clubs. For a Russian reader around 2013, the wording therefore carried both aspirational prestige and a faintly self-dramatizing, tongue-in-cheek quality.

rendering.en: Durov.com Club — Ilya Perekopsky, Vice President / Pavel Durov, President
rendering.zh: Durov.com Club——Ilya Perekopsky, Vice President / Pavel Durov, President
rendering.ja: Durov.com Club――Ilya Perekopsky, Vice President / Pavel Durov, President

Durov.com Club, Ilya Perekopsky, Vice Pr.rationale: All three versions preserve the card’s actual English wording, including the deliberately grand corporate titles and Western-campus pose. This sacrifices immediate identification of the Russian names and offices for Chinese and Japanese readers, but translating them would erase the inscription’s central social and stylistic signal.

Mail.ru.finding: Mail.ru was a Russian internet holding company (founded 1998 as an e-mail service, later Mail.ru Group, renamed VK in 2021) that by 2013 controlled or held stakes in VKontakte, Odnoklassniki and Moi Mir, plus email, ICQ and Agent messaging. For a 2013 Russian reader it connoted the incumbent, corporate, quasi-monopolist owner of the Runet's mass-audience services — in the Durov narrative, the creeping acquirer of VKontakte shares. As a proper brand it is kept untranslated in English, Chinese (Mail.ru集团 for the holding) and Japanese editions.

rendering.ja: Mail.ru

Mail.ru.rationale: Denotation and brand register are fully preserved by keeping the Latin-script name, which all three editions already use; the connotation of 'the corporate incumbent' is context-dependent but can be flagged once in zh as 集团 so readers see it is the holding company, not just the email service. Nothing is sacrificed beyond what the surrounding text supplies.

дом Зингера.finding: This is the Singer Company building at Nevsky Prospekt 28, St Petersburg (P. Syuzor, 1902–1904), a federal landmark later known to locals as Дом книги after the large bookstore that occupied it from 1938. Russians in 2013 would hear both the Art Nouveau ‘Singer’ prestige of the address and the everyday ‘House of Books’ identity; VKontakte’s offices there signalled a glamorous central-Nevsky HQ, not a generic sewing-machine firm house. It is not the demolished New York Singer Building.

rendering.zh: 圣彼得堡胜家大楼（“书籍之家”）
rendering.ja: シンガー・ハウス（「本の家」）

дом Зингера.rationale: English keeps the established landmark name Singer House; Chinese and Japanese add the House of Books tag so the Nevsky bookstore-landmark is not confused with New York’s Singer Building, sacrificing a one-word gloss for denotation.

консильери.finding: Консильери (итал. consigliere, 'советник') — третья по рангу должность в иерархии сицилийской и американской мафии: доверенное лицо и советник дона, который единственный может спорить с боссом. Для русскоязычного читателя слово почти целиком пришло через роман Марио Пьюзо «Крёстный отец» (1969) и фильм Копполы (1972); в 2010-х оно широко употреблялось иронически для обозначения узкого круга ближайших советчиков руководителя. В биографии Дурова 2013 года оно намекает, что его окружение — не просто команда, а «мафиозная» клика ближайших соратников-дон; используемое как коллективное единственное число, оно сохраняет и юмор, и оттенок закрытости.

rendering.ja: コンシリエーレ（参謀格の側近）

консильери.rationale: English keeps the loanword plural 'consiglieri', which The Godfather made standard and which preserves both denotation and the mafia connotation, sacrificing only the Russian collective-singular quirk. Japanese uses the well-established katakana コンシリエーレ from the Godfather novels, glossed briefly with 参謀格の側近 so a business reader gets the sense without a footnote. Chinese sacrifices the Italian exoticism: 军师 is the native analogue (strategist-adviser, e.g. Zhuge Liang) that a general reader instantly reads as 'trusted counsellor of a boss', keeping the insider-circle connotation and register while losing the explicit mafia frame — a literal 康西里埃里 would be opaque without a note.

Слава.finding: Слава is the familiar form of Vyacheslav (Yitzchak) Mirilashvili (b. 1984, Leningrad), son of Georgian-Jewish media magnate Mikhail Mirilashvili. In 2006 he co-founded VKontakte with Pavel Durov and Lev Leviev, served as its chairman, and his family supplied most of the initial funding, giving him the controlling stake. Around 2013 Russian readers knew him as the money behind VK — in 2013 he sold his remaining stake for roughly $1 billion — so 'Слава' in a Durov biography signals the friend with the purse who negotiated VK's valuation with investors such as DST.

rendering.zh: 斯拉瓦·米里拉什维利（维亚切斯拉夫·米里拉什维利，VK联合创始人）
rendering.ja: スラワ・ミリラシビリ（本名ヴャチェスラフ、VK共同創業者）

Слава.rationale: The bare diminutive 'Slava' conveys intimacy but identifies no one outside Russia, so the surname must be restored in all three languages; in zh and ja a brief in-line gloss of who he is replaces a footnote. The colloquial familiarity of the diminutive is sacrificed in en, partially kept via katakana スラワ in ja and 斯拉瓦 in zh.

Добромыслов.finding: A real Russian compound surname (from 'добрый' + 'мысль', literally 'kind-thought') borne by a VKontakte designer mentioned in the mock siege episode — the staged 'storming' of the VK office around Durov. Wikipedia has no article on this individual; the surname appears only in VK staff lists and press coverage. For a Russian reader around 2013 it carried a faint comic echo of its transparent etymology, but was treated purely as a proper name.
sources: web searches for 'Добромыслов ВКонтакте' — no dedicated article found

rendering.ja: ドブロミスロフ

Добромыслов.rationale: Standard transliterations in all three languages, preserving denotation and the neutral register of a serious biography; the transparent 'kind thought' etymology — only a faint humorous undertone in Russian — is sacrificed, since glossing it would over-read a walk-on name.

Андрей Лопатин.finding: Andrei Sergeyevich Lopatin is a Russian programmer, co-creator of VKontakte and Telegram, two-time world champion in competitive programming (ACM-ICPC 2000, 2001), and coach of the SPbSU competitive programming team. For a Russian reader in 2013 his name signaled elite technical pedigree — being a champion-turned-coach of one of the world's top competitive programming teams — which explained why Durov trusted him to rebuild VKontakte's engine.

rendering.en: Andrei Lopatin, a coach of Russia's champion competitive-programming team (himself a two-time ACM-ICPC world champion)
rendering.zh: 安德烈·洛帕京(两届ACM-ICPC世界冠军,俄罗斯顶尖大学生编程队教练)
rendering.ja: アンドレイ・ロパーチン(ACM-ICPC世界大会二連覇の実績を持つ、ロシアの競技プログラミング強豪チームのコーチ)

Андрей Лопатин.rationale: Preserved denotation (personal name transliteration) and added the champion/coach credential explicitly since it carries connotative weight for the source audience that a bare name transliteration would lose; sacrificed brevity to keep this context.

Усманов.finding: Это Алишер Бурханович Усманов, российский миллиардер узбекского происхождения, чьи активы включали металлургию, «Коммерсантъ», «МегаФон» и интернет-инвестиции через Mail.ru Group. Для российского читателя около 2013 года одна фамилия обозначала широко известного олигарха и влиятельного владельца капитала, стоявшего за крупным акционером «ВКонтакте», поэтому несла оттенок не только богатства, но и корпоративной власти над окружением Дурова. Употребление фамилии само по себе нейтрально по регистру, хотя контекст вызывает эти ассоциации.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/アリシェル・ウスマノフ

rendering.ja: ウスマノフ

Усманов.rationale: Сохранены принятые в каждой языковой традиции формы фамилии и ее узнаваемая отсылка к влиятельному миллиардеру; китайское «乌斯马诺夫» заменено на закрепившееся в источниках «奥斯曼诺夫». Без поясняющего имени или контекста частично утрачивается российская ассоциация с олигархической и корпоративной властью.

Равдоникас.finding: Равдоникас is a Lithuanian-origin Russian surname (standard scholarly Latinization Ravdonikas), borne in Russian Wikipedia by archaeologist Vladislav Iosifovich Ravdonikas and musicologist Feliks Vladislavovich Ravdonikas. In the 2013 Durov/VKontakte biography it denotes a living member of Durov’s inner circle nicknamed the ‘Mafia’, not those historical figures; a 2013 Russian reader would hear an uncommon Baltic-sounding family name, not a public celebrity. No dedicated Wikipedia page exists for the VK associate.

rendering.ja: ラヴドニカス

Равдоникас.rationale: Preserved denotation via the established English scholarly spelling and matching phonetic Chinese/Japanese forms already proposed; sacrificed any extra gloss of Baltic rarity or ‘Mafia’ nickname, which belongs in surrounding prose rather than the name itself.

тотем.finding: In Nikolai Kononov's 2013 biography 'Код Дурова' ('The Durov Code'), the author repeatedly calls Pavel Durov 'тотем' — a totem — to convey his role as an untouchable, worshipped icon/idol of the VKontakte community and Russian internet youth culture, someone treated with quasi-religious reverence rather than ordinary corporate-founder respect. The word evokes primitive tribal worship: a totem is not just admired but venerated as a protective, symbolic ancestor-figure of the tribe, fitting the cult-of-personality dynamic Kononov describes around Durov and his followers/employees.

rendering.ja: トーテム

тотем.rationale: All three renderings preserve the literal denotation (totem/tribal idol) and the ironic, semi-mythologizing connotation of a worshipped figurehead; register is kept serious-biographical rather than slangy, sacrificing only the specific Russian internet-culture flavor which has no direct analogue and must be inferred from context.

микроблог.finding: Здесь «микроблог» означает не отдельный сервис, а введённый «ВКонтакте» в августе 2010 года режим, который заменил прежний вид пользовательской «Стены» хронологической лентой коротких публикаций и комментариев. Для русского читателя 2013 года слово непосредственно вызывало ассоциацию с Twitter и одновременно напоминало о конфликте вокруг принудительной переделки привычной «Стены».

rendering.ja: ミニブログ型ウォール

микроблог.rationale: Все три варианта сохраняют главное различие: это новая, похожая на микроблог форма «Стены», а не самостоятельный блог-сервис. Они передают современную на тот момент ассоциацию с Twitter/微博, но саму конфликтность редизайна приходится восстанавливать из контекста.

Николай.finding: Николай refers to Nikolai Valeryevich Durov (born 1980), Pavel Durov's elder brother, a mathematician and programmer who co-founded VKontakte (2006) and later Telegram (2013), serving as VK's technical director. In the Russian source, the bare first name 'Николай' relies on immediate context (family relationship, VKontakte) for identification; a Russian reader in 2013 would instantly associate this with the Durov brothers. The Chinese Wikipedia renders him as '尼古拉·杜洛夫' and Japanese sources use 'ニコライ・ドゥーロフ', confirming established transliterations in both languages.

rendering.ja: ニコライ

Николай.rationale: Denotation is preserved exactly: the bare first name matches the source. The risk of ambiguity (mistaking him for another Nikolai) is a contextual problem solved by the surrounding sentence, not by the name token itself; adding 'Durov' here would over-translate. All three renderings use the established standard transliteration of the first name in each language.

«Мой Мир».finding: Launched in 2007 by Mail.ru (originally 'Мой мир@Mail.ru'), Moi Mir was an early integrated Russian social network combining blogging, photos, music, video, and Mail.ru Agent messaging. Around 2013, it ranked as the third-largest domestic network behind VKontakte and Odnoklassniki, but among youth and tech circles it was widely perceived as uncool, spam-ridden, and artificially inflated by forced integration with Mail.ru's email service.

rendering.ja: モイ・ミール（Moi Mir）

«Мой Мир».rationale: Preserves the established corporate brand identity in Romanized transliteration while providing glosses/qualifiers in Chinese and English to convey meaning and avoid confusion (particularly in Chinese with the video game Minecraft, commonly called 《我的世界》); sacrifices Russian orthographic flavor for readability.

Добрая машина пропаганды.finding: Navalny’s 2012 grassroots volunteer network (site Mashina.org), first named Добрая машина пропаганды and later Добрая машина правды (ДМП). He framed it as a decentralized, ‘kind’ counterpart to the state’s ‘evil propaganda machine’ (TV and official media): people spreading anti-corruption facts via social posts, leaflets, graffiti, stamped banknotes, Wi‑Fi. Launched after the 5 March 2012 Pushkin Square rally; by 2013 it had largely wound down. For a 2013 Russian reader the phrase was a named, ironic campaign title, not a generic description.

rendering.ja: 善なるプロパガンダ機械

Добрая машина пропаганды.rationale: Kept the campaign’s proper-name shape and the ironic добрый/пропаганда pairing so it stays recognizable; gave up a gloss of later rebranding as ‘Truth Machine’ and any footnote on methods. EN/ZH/JA all calque rather than localize, matching how the title was coined as a slogan.

«ВКонтакте».finding: «ВКонтакте» is Russia's largest social network, founded by Pavel Durov in 2006 in Saint Petersburg, originally positioned as a student networking site. The name literally means 'In Contact' (inspired by the Echo of Moscow radio jingle 'В полном контакте с информацией'). By 2013 it was the dominant Russian-language social platform. The company later adopted 'VK' as its international brand name (formally rebranded in 2021), but in 2013 Russian speakers still overwhelmingly used the full form «ВКонтакте». English, Chinese, and Japanese Wikipedia articles all treat 'VKontakte' as the primary romanized form with 'VK' as the recognized abbreviation.

rendering.ja: VKontakte（VK）

«ВКонтакте».rationale: Preserves the brand name as a proper noun in its internationally recognized romanized form, giving readers the abbreviation they are most likely to encounter in subsequent references. Sacrifices the literal Russian meaning ('In Contact'), which is never used as the name in any target-language context. The katakana form フコンタクテ used by Japanese Wikipedia was considered but rejected for a business biography where the Latin-script brand name is standard for international tech companies.

Шереметьевский дворец.finding: The Sheremetev Palace in St Petersburg, also known as the Fountain House (Фонтанный дом) — the 18th-century baroque palace of the Sheremetev counts on the Fontanka Embankment, now housing the Museum of Music and the Anna Akhmatova Museum. For a Russian reader in 2013 it connoted old aristocratic Petersburg prestige and high culture, an evocative, slightly ironic setting for negotiations over a scrappy internet company. It has nothing to do with Sheremetyevo airport (Шереметьево), though the near-identical root invites confusion, especially in transliteration.

rendering.ja: シェレメーチエフ宮殿（フォンターンカの「噴水の家」）

Шереметьевский дворец.rationale: Keeps the family-name denotation while glossing the locally famous 'Fountain House' alias once, which anchors the place for foreign readers and disambiguates it from Sheremetyevo airport; sacrifices some of the effortless instant recognition a Russian reader has. Standard transliterations (Sheremetev / 谢列梅捷夫 / シェレメーチエフ) are preserved.

филфак.finding: Филфак is the standard colloquial Russian student abbreviation for факультет филологии (Faculty of Philology), here referring to Saint Petersburg State University's Philological Faculty, where Pavel Durov actually studied. The clipped form is generic Soviet/Russian campus slang (like матфак, истфак) signaling insider student vernacular rather than formal bureaucratic naming; it carries no negative connotation, just informality and a sense of everyday student speech.

rendering.en: the philology department (at St Petersburg State University)
rendering.zh: 圣彼得堡国立大学语文系（俄语学生口语简称“菲尔法克”）
rendering.ja: サンクトペテルブルク国立大学文学部

филфак.rationale: English and Japanese keep denotation and institutional register clear (formal biography tone), sacrificing the colloquial campus-slang flavor; Chinese rendering adds the institution plus a brief nod to the informal Russian abbreviation to hint at student vernacular without a full footnote.

Андрей Рогозов.finding: Андрей Олегович Рогозов（1987年生まれ）は、2007年にVKontakteへ加わった初期の主要開発者で、のちに開発責任者、さらに同サービスの経営幹部となった人物である。2013年頃のロシア語読者には、著名人というより、パーヴェル・ドゥーロフの周囲でVKを技術的に築いた中核メンバーとして受け取られる名前だった。後年の肩書きは資料間で「CEO」と「managing director」の揺れがあるが、本人は国際向けに「Andrew Rogozov」も使用している。

rendering.ja: アンドレイ・ロゴゾフ

Андрей Рогозов.rationale: 各言語で人物の同一性を安定して追える表記を優先し、英語では本人の国際向け表記「Andrew Rogozov」を採用した。中国語と日本語では標準的なロシア人名の音写を保ち、初期VK技術者という含意は名前自体には付加しない。

ВКонтакте.finding: ВКонтакте (VKontakte) is the Russian social network Pavel Durov launched in 2006 in St. Petersburg, initially pitched as a network for Russian university students before becoming the largest social network in the Russian-speaking internet. The name reworks the Echo of Moscow radio slogan 'в полном контакте с информацией' (in full contact with information), so to a Russian reader the word carried both the literal sense 'in contact' and the everyday meaning of being connected/online. Around 2013, before the 2014 Mail.ru Group takeover and the later consolidation under the 'VK' brand, Russians knew and said the full name 'ВКонтакте'; the international Latin name was VKontakte, with 'VK' only as a short form.

rendering.ja: VKontakte（フコンタクテ）

ВКонтакте.rationale: All three audiences already know the service under its Latin brand 'VKontakte', so I keep that denotation and the brand's recognizability; the parenthetical short form 'VK' (en/zh) or the katakana 'フコンタクテ' (ja) carries pronunciation/abbreviation at the cost of the Russian connotation 'in contact', which I drop as untranslatable without a footnote.

Тотем.finding: Тотем ('Totem') was the online nickname/handle Pavel Durov used on the spbgu.ru (Saint Petersburg State University) student forums before founding VKontakte. It functioned as a personal pseudonym in the pseudonymous forum culture of the Russian internet in the mid-2000s, signaling a chosen online identity rather than any literal totemic/tribal symbol. It carries no strong ideological or humorous connotation beyond being a memorable handle; its significance is purely as a biographical detail marking Durov's early online persona.

rendering.ja: トーテム（ハンドルネーム）

Тотем.rationale: Preserved denotation (the actual nickname, transliterated/kept recognizable) and clarified via gloss that it is a forum handle, sacrificing any symbolic 'totem' connotation that could mislead readers into thinking it's a cultural object rather than a username.

Зингер.finding: The Singer House (Дом компании «Зингер»), built 1902–1904 on Nevsky Prospekt 28 by architect Pavel Suzor for the Singer Sewing Machine Company's Russian headquarters, is a landmark Art Nouveau building famous for its glass dome. Since 1938 it has housed the 'Dom Knigi' bookstore, and its upper floors were rented by VKontakte's early offices, giving it a mythic status as the birthplace of the Russian Facebook. For a Russian reader in 2013, naming 'Зингер' evokes both imperial-era architectural grandeur and the romantic startup lore of VK beginning in a historic, almost incongruously ornate building rather than a modern tech campus.

rendering.en: the Singer House (the historic Singer sewing-machine building on Nevsky Prospekt)
rendering.zh: 辛格大楼(涅瓦大街上的历史建筑,原辛格缝纫机公司总部)
rendering.ja: シンガー・ハウス(ネフスキー大通りにあるかつてのシンガー社ビル)

Зингер.rationale: Preserved denotation (specific landmark building) and added a brief gloss so foreign readers grasp its historic/architectural significance, sacrificing the compact one-word familiarity a Russian reader has.

«Одноклассниках».finding: The prepositional form of Одноклассники (ok.ru), the Russian social network launched 26 March 2006 by Albert Popkov as a Classmates.com analogue for reconnecting schoolmates. By 2013 it had over 200 million registered accounts and was VK/VKontakte’s main domestic rival, later under Mail.ru/VK. For a 2013 Russian reader it named a mass, slightly older/provincial-coded network, not the common noun “classmates.”

rendering.ja: オドノクラスニキ

«Одноклассниках».rationale: Keep the Latin brand in English; give Chinese readers a Classmates-style analogue plus the proper name; use established katakana in Japanese. Literal “classmates” is sacrificed so the word is not read as a common noun.

Гришин.finding: Dmitry Sergeyevich Grishin (born 1978) was co-founder, CEO, and later chairman of the board of directors of Mail.ru Group (later renamed VK). He is credited as the visionary who identified online games and communications as key growth areas for the company, though his role was far broader than 'head of the gaming unit.' In the Durov/VKontakte narrative he is the antagonist because Mail.ru Group, as VKontakte's largest shareholder, pushed for control over the social network, culminating in Durov's eventual ouster. A Russian reader in 2013 would have recognized 'Гришин' immediately as the top executive of Mail.ru and the corporate counterweight to Durov.

rendering.ja: グリシン

Гришин.rationale: All three renderings preserve denotation (the surname as a proper noun) and are consistent with existing usage in each language's Wikipedia. The English and Japanese forms sacrifice nothing; the Chinese 格里申 is the established transliteration already used in the Chinese Wikipedia article on Mail.ru. No connotation or register is lost because the surname alone carries no evaluative charge in any of the three languages.

«Одноклассники».finding: Odnoklassniki (odnoklassniki.ru, later ok.ru) is a Russian social network founded by Albert Popkov in March 2006, built around finding former school classmates. It targeted an older, non-tech-savvy audience and became hugely popular in the ex-USSR; by 2007 it was Russia's top social network, until VKontakte overtook it in December 2008. In a 2013 biography of Durov it is the main early rival VK beat, and for Russian readers its name instantly evokes 'classmates,' with a slightly mass-market, older-generation connotation compared with VK's student cool. All three major Wikipedias keep the name as 'Odnoklassniki' (ja: オドノクラスニキ), so transliteration is the established cross-lingual identity.

rendering.ja: オドノクラスニキ（「同級生」の意）

«Одноклассники».rationale: Keeps denotation and the proper-noun identity that all encyclopedic tradition uses, adding a one-time meaning gloss ('classmates') so the name's point — a school-reunion site — survives for readers with no Russian; the older-generation, mass-market connotation versus VK is sacrificed, as it must be carried by context rather than the name. Avoids invented brand-style translations like 同学网, which do not exist as established usage.

Лев Левиев.finding: Это Лев Бинзумович Левиев (род. 1984), российско-израильский предприниматель, школьный товарищ Вячеслава Мирилашвили по американской школе в Герцлии. Он стал третьим сооснователем «ВКонтакте», вложил средства в проект и до апреля 2012 года отвечал за оперативное управление компанией. Для российского читателя 2013 года имя обозначало молодого, сравнительно непубличного совладельца VK, а не гораздо более известного алмазного магната Льва Авнеровича Леваева.

rendering.zh: 列夫·宾祖莫维奇·列维耶夫
rendering.ja: レフ・ビンズモヴィチ・レヴィエフ

Лев Левиев.rationale: Полное имя сохраняет точную денотацию и предотвращает смешение с алмазным магнатом; ценой становится небольшая экспликация по сравнению с краткой формой русского оригинала. Во всех трёх языках выбран нейтральный биографический регистр.

Гриз.finding: Не удалось установить личность Гриза по доступным источникам. В русскоязычном интернете и биографиях Павла Дурова/Вячеслава Мирилашвили (Slava) фигура с такой фамилией/прозвищем не фиксируется. Учитывая контекст эмиграции Мирилашвили в Израиль в 1990-е годы, Гриз — вероятно, частное лицо (возможно, адвокат или знакомый семьи), не публичная персона. Для русскоязычного читателя 2013 года это был неизвестный второстепенный персонаж, упомянутый по фамилии без пояснений.

rendering.ja: グリズ

Гриз.rationale: Сохраняется денотативная функция (фамилия/имя частного лица), коннотация и регистр не передаются, так как личность не установлена; в en используется транслитерация, в zh — стандартная транскрипция кириллицы, в ja — катакана.

троллить.finding: Троллинг — деятельность по написанию провокационных, издевательских или откровенно нелепых сообщений с целью вызвать конфликт, эмоциональную реакцию или просто позабавиться. В русском Runet 2000-х это слово охватывало широкий диапазон: от лёгкого дружеского подшучивания и подкалывания в чатах/форумах до организованной травли и манипуляции. Оно уже устоялось как заимствование от английского 'troll' и воспринималось скорее нейтрально-иронично, а не исключительно как злонамеренное действие.

rendering.zh: 网络找乐子挑衅（网络戏弄）
rendering.ja: からかう（ネットで挑発する）

троллить.rationale: Сохраняю денотативное значение (провокация ради реакции) во всех языках; для en использую уже устоявшийся англицизм 'troll', сохраняя регистр и коннотацию напрямую, так как термин заимствован из английского. Для zh и ja жертвую точным сленговым колоритом 2000-х Runet в пользу описательного эквивалента, понятного без сноски, чтобы передать двойственность (дружеское подкалывание/организованная провокация).

люди в черном.finding: The phrase evokes the Hollywood 'Men in Black' franchise (secret agents in black suits/sunglasses) and was applied ironically to Durov's security guards and dark-suited entourage at VKontakte, known for their strict all-black dress code and enforcer-like presence during office raids and paper-plane money-drops. In Russian usage the phrase also puns on 'люди в черном' as mourners/undertakers, reinforcing a menacing, quasi-comic aura around Durov's protective circle described in the 2013 biography.

rendering.ja: 「黒服の男たち」（メン・イン・ブラック）

люди в черном.rationale: Preserves the film allusion and ironic register in all three; English keeps it directly via capitalization, Chinese keeps both the film-derived idiom and its literal 'black-clad guards' sense via parenthetical gloss, Japanese keeps register with a business-appropriate phrasing plus explicit film reference for clarity, sacrificing the mourning double meaning which doesn't map well cross-culturally.

гопников.finding: In post-Soviet Russia, 'gopnik' refers to delinquent, working-class street youth typically associated with tracksuits, aggressive posturing, petty street shakedowns (street muggings/harassment), and hostility toward intellectuals, hipsters, and Westernized subcultures. Around 2013, the term functioned both as a sociological descriptor of post-Soviet urban blight and as a common derogatory label for aggressive street thugs or hooligans. In Durov's biographical context, it signifies raw street-level criminal element and uncivilized public space from which digital or intellectual spaces offered an escape.

rendering.ja: 街の不良グループ

гопников.rationale: Preserved the immediate social menace, criminal connotation, and readable register across general readership; sacrificed the uniquely Russian aesthetic (tracksuits, sunflower seeds) because borrowing 'gopniks' directly confuses general English/Japanese readers without encyclopedic glossing.

рунета.finding: Рунет is a blend of 'ru' (Russia/Russian domain code) + 'net': the Russian-language internet as a cultural and linguistic community rather than merely servers in Russia, spanning the former USSR and diaspora (ru.wikipedia article 'Рунет'). Around 2013 Russian was the second most-used language online, and for a Russian reader in the VK era 'Рунет' carried a sense of a distinct domestic digital world with its own culture, celebrities (like Durov), search engine (Yandex), and social networks — a term of insider pride, roughly 'the Russian web' as a place, not just a market. The English Wikipedia article 'Runet' confirms the term is established in English as 'Runet'; the Chinese Wikipedia uses 'Runet' directly (俄语互联网); Japanese Wikipedia has no established equivalent and ルネット collides with unrelated words (lunette, a company).

rendering.ja: ルーネット（ロシア語圏インターネット）

рунета.rationale: For English and Chinese, the established forms keep the insider-culture connotation and denotation with a minimal in-line gloss; for Japanese, where ルネット is ambiguous and unfamiliar, I foreground a descriptive phrase and demote the transliteration, preserving denotation and biography register while sacrificing the native-speaker compactness of the original.

Цыплухин.finding: Владислав Цыплухин was VKontakte's press secretary / head of its press service (руководитель пресс-службы) during Pavel Durov's tenure; he appears in the 2010s record as the company's public-facing spokesperson, e.g. explaining Durov's Victory Day posts and responding to piracy accusations. Russian Wikipedia articles on Durov and VKontakte cite him in exactly that role, and he later became head of the 'Комитет' publishing house and product director at Coub. For a 2013 Russian reader he connoted the official, polished face of the network rather than an inner-circle developer: a corporate mouthpiece in the cherry-juice anecdote.

rendering.ja: ツィプルヒン

Цыплухин.rationale: All three preserve denotation (a standard name transliteration already used for this person in each language's press); the role is carried by the surrounding text ('PR person', 'пресс-секретарь') rather than by the name itself, so nothing is lost that the name alone can convey.

Мильнер.finding: This is Юрий Борисович (Бенционович) Мильнер (b. 1961), the Soviet-born, Moscow-raised technology investor who in the 2000s founded and ran the investment fund Digital Sky Technologies (DST Global / Mail.ru Group), and who was pivotal to VKontakte's corporate history alongside Alisher Usmanov. For a Russian reader circa 2013, the bare surname Мильнер unambiguously denoted this celebrity venture capitalist — famous for early stakes in Facebook, Groupon, Zynga, Twitter and for the Breakthrough Prize — not any lesser-known bearer of the name. English, Chinese and Japanese publics already know him under a stabilized transcription as Yuri Milner / 尤里·米尔纳 / ユーリ・ミルナー, rather than by surname alone.

rendering.ja: ユーリ・ミルナー

Мильнер.rationale: The surname alone is unambiguous to a Russian reader but opaque elsewhere; supplying the conventional full name preserves denotation and the name by which each audience already knows this famous investor, at the cost of the bare-surname brevity and intimacy of the original.

рунет.finding: Runet is the informal, widely-used term for the Russian-language segment of the internet — sites, communities, and culture primarily in Russian, not limited to Russia geographically (includes diaspora, ex-USSR states). By 2013 it was a common colloquial coinage (blend of 'Russian' + 'internet'), carrying a sense of a distinct cultural/linguistic online space with its own slang, memes, and identity, similar in spirit to how 'Anglophone internet' or 'Chinese internet' might be discussed, but the term itself is a recognized proper-noun-like brand used in media, awards ('Премия Рунета'), and law discussions.

rendering.ja: ルネット（ロシア語圏インターネット）

рунет.rationale: Preserve the established loanword/brand-like status (denotation and recognizability) already used by EN/ZH/JA teams; sacrifice some connotative flavor of casual Russian slang since the term itself functions as a quasi-proper noun even in Russian.

бар «Идиот».finding: The bar «Идиот» is a well-known St Petersburg establishment on the Fontanka River embankment, named after Dostoevsky's novel 'The Idiot'. In the 2000s–2010s it was a popular gathering place for the city's creative and IT intelligentsia. For a Russian reader around 2013 the name immediately evoked both the Dostoevsky reference and the bar's status as a hip, slightly bohemian venue; the word 'идиот' carries the same double edge in Russian as 'idiot' does in English — a literary title and a common insult — which is part of the bar's ironic charm. Wikipedia does not have a dedicated article for the bar itself, so details are drawn from general knowledge of St Petersburg cultural life and the Durov biography context.

rendering.ja: バー「白痴」

бар «Идиот».rationale: In all three languages the bar name is rendered using the established local title of Dostoevsky's novel (English 'The Idiot', Chinese '白痴', Japanese '白痴'), which preserves the literary allusion — the primary connotation a Russian reader would register. The ironic/insult edge of the bare word is sacrificed in zh and ja, where the novel title is the dominant association, but this is acceptable because the biographical context makes the venue's cultural cachet clear. Transliteration was rejected because it would obscure the allusion entirely.

трэша.finding: Russian internet slang 'трэш' is a direct borrowing of English 'trash', used in the 2000s–2010s Ru-net not to mean literal garbage but a genre/aesthetic of deliberately shocking, trashy, provocative content — the register of what Anton Loginov later dubbed the 'нижний интернет' and of early trash-streaming. Calling something 'трэш' carried an ironic, knowing connoisseurship: it is edgy and transgressive rather than merely vulgar, and Durov's enjoyment of it reads as deliberately lowbrow. English 'trash culture' is the established cognate, with the same ironic appreciation built in.

rendering.ja: トラッシュ（低俗・衝撃系）コンテンツ

трэша.rationale: All three keep the borrowed-English flavor and the shock/edgy register rather than literal garbage; the glossing additions in zh and ja trade brevity for legibility, since bare 垃圾 would read as 'worthless' and lose the ironic-genre connotation.

Мирилашвили.finding: Вячеслав (Ицхак) Михайлович Мирилашвили, род. 1984 в Ленинграде — однокурсник Павла Дурова по СПбГУ, в 2006 году сооснователь «ВКонтакте» (вместе с Львом Левиевым и Дуровым), председатель компании и держатель контрольного пакета; в 2013 продал оставшиеся акции примерно за миллиард долларов и живёт в Израиле. Сын грузинско-еврейского бизнесмена Михаила Мирилашвили. Для русского читателя 2013 года фамилия обозначала «деньги и контрольный пакет ВК»: малоизвестного публике, но ключевого акционера, чей выход из компании совпал с кризисом вокруг Дурова.

rendering.ja: ミリラシュヴィリ

Мирилашвили.rationale: Прозрачная фонетическая транслитерация во всех трёх языках, совпадающая с употреблением в английской Википедии; сохранена денотация и нейтральный регистр деловой биографии, от коннотаций фамилии (грузинско-еврейское происхождение, олигархический флёр) для нерусского читателя пришлось отказаться — они восстанавливаются только контекстом.

Одноклассники.finding: Launched in March 2006 by Albert Popkov, Odnoklassniki (literally 'Classmates', later rebranded as OK.ru) was the pioneering social network in the Runet and VKontakte's chief domestic rival. By around 2013, it had been absorbed into Mail.ru Group (Yuri Milner/Alisher Usmanov) and carried a distinct demographic and cultural reputation: heavily focused on older generations, provincial Russia, nostalgic school reunions, and aggressive monetization (such as paid registration and paid digital gifts), contrasting sharply with Durov's younger, tech-savvy, and urban VKontakte user base.

rendering.ja: Odnoklassniki（オドノクラスニキ）

Одноклассники.rationale: Preserves the proper proprietary brand identity in all languages while sacrificing immediate literal transparency in EN/JA, mitigating it in ZH and JA by supplying a parenthetical semantic gloss ('同学网', evoking China's Classmates/Renren culture) and standard phonetic katakana guidance respectively.

День города.finding: In post-Soviet Russia, 'День города' (City Day) is a ubiquitous annual municipal festival marked by massive street celebrations, concerts, fairs, and fireworks. In Saint Petersburg, it commemorates the founding of the city by Peter the Great on May 27, 1703, typically celebrated on the nearest weekend in late May with crowded avenues, open-air drinking, and revellers filling Nevsky Prospekt—famously intersecting with VKontakte's Singer House headquarters and Durov's airplane-throwing stunt in May 2012.

rendering.ja: 市の日（サンクトペテルブルク創設記念日）

День города.rationale: Preserved the civic institution and cultural weight of the holiday; in English 'City Day' is standard journalism style with contextual St. Petersburg clarity, Chinese uses the established term '城市日' without bloating, while Japanese clarifies the nature of the celebration ('創設記念日') to prevent misinterpreting it as an ordinary public holiday or municipal meeting day in a serious business biography.
